_why: What lib/verbs/ar.py needs and no row of dict/ar.db says: how the edition respells Wiktionary's romanisation, and which Arabic words are prepositions. Both are the conventions of docs/lang/ar.md written down as tables, so the next editor changes a line here and not the code.
_roman: Wiktionary romanises Arabic with ʔ ʕ ḵ ḡ, and docs/lang/ar.md writes ʾ ʿ ḫ ġ -- the rest (ā ī ū, ṯ ḏ š ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ ḥ, j q) is the same letter in both. Counted over the verb rows the recipe reads (the romanization row, and the roman of the non-past and noun-from-verb rows): ʕ in 3648, ʔ in 3368, ḵ in 1778, ḡ in 1120, and no other letter outside the edition's set. So raʔā, ʔirāda and yaḵruju become raʾā, irāda and yaḫruju, as the fixture book writes them.
_drop_initial: Hamza is never written at the start of a word (docs/lang/ar.md: `amal`, not `ʾamal`), and Wiktionary writes it there every time: ʔarāda, ʔirāda, ʔaktubu. Only at the start of the string or after a space -- inside a word it is a consonant the reader needs (raʾā, ruʾya).
_prepositions: The words that may stand after the + of a governed preposition, bare (no harakat, no tatweel) and compared bare, so إِلَى, إلى and بِـ are found as written. The +obj template of a Wiktionary sense names its object as a case (acc), a preposition (:إِلَى) or something else entirely -- أَنْ with the subjunctive 17 times, نَفْسَهُ, a pronoun -- and only the prepositions are what the extra is for (docs/lang/ar.md: the preposition the verb governs, where it does not simply take a direct object). Counted over every obj: tag of the verbs: على 367, ب 313, إلى 230, من 151, عن 143, في 129, ل 108, مع 17, بين 9, حول 5, then single figures; the rest of the list is the doc's own never-gloss prepositions.
